findings.text: The first sentence tells a newcomer what Athena is, so the page starts well. The next two paragraphs explain that this page is a study of a different project, which heads off confusion about why a page on Athena's site is about firstmate.
findings.source: Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository.

findings.text: The header says why the page matters: it shows off Athena's traced reading of another project. Athena's own value gets one sentence, though, and everything after the header is about firstmate. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena gets little more than the lede and a link.
findings.source: Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files.

findings.text: The header links straight to a concrete next step, and the Next steps section gives a repo link, an install command and an example command, so the reader knows what to do next.
findings.source: Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself

findings.text: The install step assumes the reader already has a checkout but gives no clone command. It also says nothing about prerequisites such as a Rust toolchain or access to AI models, so a newcomer may get stuck before trying `athena ask`.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh"

findings.text: The 'Start here' section gets dense quickly: exit codes, 'places', 'guarded fast-forward' and 'shared project lock' all appear early. Some are defined only in the Glossary further down, and 'PR' is never spelled out until there. A non-specialist will struggle with the walkthrough.
findings.source: Start here: "Spawning moves the item to In flight and creates an isolated worktree for the worker. If every place of a declared capacity is held, the spawn exits 75 and the item stays queued."

findings.text: The 'Words used first' list defines terms using other words that have not been defined yet. 'local-only ship' is used before 'ship' is explained, and 'merge authority' is never given its own definition.
findings.source: Words used first: "local-only landing … The last step of a local-only ship"

findings.text: Some glossary entries are thin or circular. 'ship' is described by where it is mentioned rather than what it is, and 'stale wake' is defined with the word 'wake', which is never explained.
findings.source: Glossary: "ship — A kind of task, named next to scouts." and "stale wake — A wake after which the agent inspects a worker"

findings.text: The page is honest about its limits: claims come from reading the code, not running it, and gaps such as the undefined 'in scope' are stated plainly. That builds trust with a careful reader.
findings.source: Limits of this study: "This study read the pinned tree only… no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read."

findings.text: The 'About this page' section and the footer point to an internal folder path. This means nothing to a newcomer, and there is no link to the folder.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from"
